title: How to Transfer Money from Abroad to Indonesia
summary: Learn how to transfer money from abroad to Indonesia safely and easily. Step-by-step guide covering bank transfers, apps, and smart tips for sending money home.
body_markdown:
[Living Abroad](https://blog.transfez.com/en/living-abroad/)


Whether you are working overseas, studying in another country, or simply helping family back home, sending money to Indonesia is something millions of people do every single month. But if you have ever stared at a bank form or an app screen wondering what to fill in next, you are not alone.[The Indonesian diaspora](https://blog.transfez.com/en/indonesian-diaspora-who-they-are-and-why-they-matter/) is massive, and navigating international remittance can feel confusing the first time around.


The good news? It is actually much simpler than it looks. Once you understand the basic process and your available options, sending money home becomes as routine as buying groceries. Let this guide walk you through everything you need to know.

##


**Why People Send Money to Indonesia from Abroad**


The reasons are as varied as the people doing it. Some send money to support parents or siblings. Others pay for a child’s school fees or help cover medical costs. Some are freelancers or remote workers receiving payments from international clients. Whatever your reason, the need is real and the demand is huge.


###


**1. Family Support and Remittances**


A large portion of international transfers to Indonesia are personal remittances, money sent by migrant workers to their families. This is one of the most common use cases globally, and Indonesia consistently ranks among the top remittance-receiving countries in Southeast Asia.


###


**2. Business and Freelance Payments**


Many Indonesian professionals work remotely for foreign companies or clients. Receiving payment from abroad and funneling it into an Indonesian bank account is a regular need for this growing group.


###


**3. Investment and Property**


Some Indonesians living overseas send money home to invest in property, business ventures, or savings accounts. Understanding the transfer process matters a lot in these cases because larger amounts involve more documentation.


##


**What You Need Before You Start**


Before you make your first transfer, gather the right information. Missing one detail can delay your transaction or, worse, send money to the wrong account. Here is a quick checklist to keep handy.


###


**1. Recipient’s Bank Details**


You will need the full name on the account, the bank name, the account number, and the bank branch. For international transfers, you may also need the bank’s *SWIFT code* or *BIC* . Every major Indonesian bank has one, so a quick search on the bank’s official website will get you this.


###


**2. Your Own Identification**


Most services will ask for a valid ID, a passport works well, and sometimes proof of your address in the country you are sending from. This is standard anti-money-laundering practice, so do not be surprised when asked.


###


**3. Source of Funds (for Larger Transfers)**


If you are sending a significant amount, some providers or banks may ask you to show where the money comes from. A payslip, employment letter, or bank statement usually covers this requirement.


##


**Main Ways to Transfer Money from Abroad to Indonesia**


There is no single best method for everyone. Your ideal option depends on where you are sending from, how quickly the recipient needs the funds, and what is most convenient for you. Here are the most common channels people use.


###


**1. International Bank Wire Transfer**


This is the classic method. You walk into your local bank or use its online banking portal, enter the recipient’s bank details including the *SWIFT code* , and initiate a wire transfer. It is reliable and widely accepted, but processing can take anywhere from one to five business days depending on the banks involved.


Banks often require more documentation and the process can feel bureaucratic. That said, for very large or formal transfers, bank wires remain a trusted option.


###


**2. Online Remittance Apps and Services**


This is where most people are heading these days. Dedicated remittance platforms and fintech apps let you send money from your phone or computer without stepping into a branch. They tend to process transfers faster and with a smoother user experience. Transfez, for example, is specifically built for transfers involving Indonesia, making the process straightforward for Indonesians abroad.


To use these services, you typically create an account, verify your identity once, link a funding source like a bank account or debit card, and then send money whenever you need to.


###


**3. Money Transfer Operators (MTOs)**


Traditional money transfer operators have physical agent locations around the world. The recipient in Indonesia can pick up cash at a local agent point. This works especially well when the recipient does not have a bank account or needs cash urgently.


###


**4. Peer-to-Peer and Multi-Currency Platforms**


Some platforms match your outgoing currency with someone else’s incoming currency, effectively swapping funds without a traditional international wire. These can offer competitive terms but may have limits on how much you can send at one time.


##


**Step-by-Step: How to Send Money to Indonesia Using an App**


Using a remittance app is often the most convenient route. Here is a simple walkthrough of how the process typically works.


1. **Download and register:** Create your account with the app of your choice. You will need to provide basic personal information.
2. **Verify your identity:** Upload a photo of your ID or passport. Most apps complete this within minutes to a few hours.
3. **Add your recipient:** Enter the recipient’s full name, Indonesian bank name, and account number. Double-check everything before saving.
4. **Enter the transfer amount:** Type in how much you want to send. The app will show you how much the recipient gets in Indonesian *Rupiah* (IDR).
5. **Choose your payment method:** Fund the transfer using your local bank account, debit card, or sometimes a digital wallet.
6. **Confirm and send:** Review the details one more time, then confirm. You will usually receive a confirmation email or notification immediately.
7. **Track the transfer:** Most apps provide a tracking feature so you and your recipient can follow the progress in real time.


##


**Practical Tips to Make Your Transfer Smoother**


A little preparation goes a long way. These tips will help you avoid common hiccups.


- **Always double-check the account number.** A wrong digit means the money lands in the wrong account, and recovery can be slow and stressful.
- **Verify the SWIFT code** directly on the recipient bank’s official website, not just from memory.
- Send a small test transfer first if it is your first time using a new platform or sending to a new recipient.
- Keep a record of every transaction, including confirmation numbers and timestamps. This is useful if anything needs to be followed up.
- Check if your recipient’s bank has any incoming international transfer limits or requires prior notification for large amounts.
- Building[strong financial literacy habits](https://blog.transfez.com/en/why-financial-literacy-is-important/) will help you make smarter decisions every time you send money abroad.


##


**Common Indonesian Banks That Accept International Transfers**


Most major Indonesian banks are set up to receive international wire transfers without any special arrangements needed on the recipient’s end. Some of the most commonly used include BCA, BNI, BRI, Mandiri, CIMB Niaga, and Danamon. Each has its own *SWIFT code* , so confirm the correct one before initiating a transfer.


Recipients should also make sure their account is active and not dormant, as inactive accounts can sometimes block incoming transfers or trigger delays.


##


**Things to Watch Out For**


International transfers are generally safe when you use established, reputable services. Still, there are a few things worth being careful about.


- Avoid sharing your transfer confirmation details publicly or with strangers.
- Be cautious of third parties offering to send money on your behalf, use official apps and channels directly.
- If a deal or service sounds too good to be true, it probably warrants extra scrutiny.
- Keep your app and device secure with a strong password and two-factor authentication where available.
